newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST - Auto strikes hurt US Apr industry output.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Auto strikes hurt US Apr industry output.

text.p: Strikes at some General Motors Corp and Chrysler Corp plants depressed U.S. industrial production in April, but excluding the impact of the auto industry work stoppages, U.S. industrial production remained quite strong, economists said.
Economists polled by Reuters estimated, on average, that industrial production increased a slight 0.2 percent in April after a robust 0.9 percent increase in March.
Meanwhile, capacity utilization, the portion of the nation's mines, utilities and factories employed in that production, remained level at 84.1, they said.

"The industrial production number is being held back by the auto strikes," said Elliott Platt, managing director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette. "But when people look at manufacturing ex-autos, they'll find the number is pretty strong."
Platt estimated that with the auto industry factored out, industrial production rose 0.8 percent in April.

One result of this differentiation could be that the bond market might, at first glance, view the April industrial production data due on Thursday, May 15, at 0915 EDT/1315 GMT as constructive for the credit markets, Platt said.
"But the re-think will be less constructive," he said.

Deborah Johnson, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, also estimates that U.S. industrial production rose 0.2 percent in April. She said the slowdown from a 0.9 percent rise in March was largely due to the auto strikes.
"If you exclude that, manufacturing is pretty solid," she said. "You have a lot of productivity-led growth."
Johnson said productivity-led growth is good news for the credit markets.
"Productivity-led growth is not inflationaary," said Johnson.

Johnson's forecast is for 2.5 percent inflation in 1997 as measured by the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and for 2.0 percent inflation in 1998. The core CPI, the CPI without its more volatile energy and food components, should rise two percent in 1997, she said.
Peter D'Antonio, senior economist at Citicorp Global Finance, estimated that production was flat in April and that capacity utilization slipped to 83.8 from 84.1 in March.
"The number will be very low because of autos," said D'Antonio. "The strike probably subtracted either five-tenths of a percent or six-tenths of a percent from production."
Platt said the strong underlying industrial production numbers fit the general story of inventory buildup and some strength in business spending on plants and equipment.
The first quarter saw relatively strong investment in plants and equipment, most of it imported, said Platt.

"This time more of that will be domestically produced, so we should see a couple more months of strong industrial production," he said. "In the late summer and early fall, businesses will realize that the front end of the economy -- housing and consumer spending -- is slowing down and that businesses have built inventories excessively."
